column2: You have configured Identity-Aware Proxy for a web application behind a global Application Load Balancer. Users report they can access the application even when not meeting the access level requirements. You need to troubleshoot this issue. What should you verify first?
column3: Verify that the backend VMs have public IP addresses disabled, since IAP cannot enforce access policies when backends are directly accessible.
column4: Verify that the IAP OAuth consent screen is configured for external users, which is required for access level conditions to be properly evaluated.
column5: Verify that the access level is set in the organizational access policy, not a scoped project or folder policy, since IAP only supports organization-level access levels.
column6: Verify that Cloud Armor security policies are configured on the load balancer to work in conjunction with IAP access level enforcement.
column8: IAP requires access levels to be set in the organizational access policy. Scoped policies (at project or folder level) are not supported by IAP. If access levels are defined in scoped policies, IAP cannot enforce them, causing the observed behavior. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iap/docs/cloud-iap-context-aware-access-howto

column2: Your security team needs to be notified immediately when specific critical security events appear in Cloud Audit Logs, such as when a service account key is created or when IAM permissions are modified. You want to configure alerting that directly scans log entries and extracts relevant field data to include in notifications. What should you do?
column3: Configure Cloud Monitoring to monitor the system-defined log_entry_count metric and filter by the specific log types.
column4: Create a log-based counter metric and configure an alerting policy with a threshold of 1.
column5: Create a log-based alerting policy using Logs Explorer with label extraction configured via the Monitoring API.
column6: Configure a SQL-based alerting policy using Log Analytics to run queries every minute.
column8: Log-based alerting policies scan individual log entries for specific phrases and can extract data from log entries using the Monitoring API. This approach provides immediate notification when matching entries appear and supports including extracted log data in the notification. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/alerting/log-based-alerts

column2: You are configuring an Event Threat Detection custom module to detect when Compute Engine instances are created in unauthorized regions. You plan to use the gcloud CLI to create the custom module. What must you include in the JSON template to ensure the custom module generates findings with appropriate context for your security team?
column3: Metadata section containing severity level, description, and recommendation fields with your custom values.
column4: A YARA-L rule that defines the detection logic for unauthorized regions alongside the module template.
column5: An API key for the Security Command Center API to authenticate the custom module creation request.
column6: Detection parameters only, as the metadata is automatically generated based on the module type selected.
column8: The metadata section of the JSON template defines the severity (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL), description of the threat, and recommendation for remediation. Module templates let you define the severity of threats and provide custom remediation steps to help security teams fix issues. This context is essential for proper triage and response. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: You want to proactively hunt for threats in your Google Cloud environment by searching historical logs against newly discovered IoCs from threat intelligence feeds. The IoCs were added to Google SecOps after the initial logs were ingested. How should you search for these IoCs in historical event data?
column3: Create a new data ingestion pipeline to re-ingest historical logs so they are matched against the current IoC list.
column4: Configure real-time IoC matching and wait for the next occurrence of the IoCs in new incoming logs.
column5: Export all historical logs to BigQuery and run SQL queries with the IoC values against the exported data.
column6: Run a retrohunt using YARA-L detection rules that include the new IoCs to search across existing data in Google SecOps.
column8: A retrohunt lets you use detection rules to search for detections throughout existing data in Google SecOps. This capability allows you to compare and perform retrohunts of historical event data with newly enriched logs, which is essential for proactive threat hunting when new IoCs are discovered. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: You have built a Looker Studio security dashboard connected to BigQuery containing Security Command Center findings. Executive stakeholders require weekly PDF reports summarizing critical and high severity findings. The reports must be automatically delivered every Monday morning without manual intervention. You need to implement the most efficient solution. What should you do?
column3: Embed the Looker Studio dashboard in an internal web portal and instruct executives to access it directly each Monday to view current findings.
column4: Train an analyst to manually export the dashboard to PDF every Monday and email it to executives using their corporate email client.
column5: Create a Cloud Scheduler job that triggers a Cloud Function to export the dashboard as PDF using the Looker Studio API and email it via SendGrid.
column6: Configure a scheduled delivery in Looker Studio to email a PDF of the dashboard to the executive distribution list with a weekly recurrence set for Monday mornings.
column8: Looker Studio's scheduled delivery feature automates the generation and distribution of PDF reports at specified intervals. This built-in capability eliminates manual effort and ensures stakeholders receive consistent, timely security reports. Filters can be applied to focus on critical and high severity findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker/docs/studio/schedule-automatic-report-delivery

column2: You are implementing a threat detection solution that correlates IAM audit logs stored in BigQuery with threat intelligence data. The solution must support both ad-hoc analyst queries and automated scheduled detections that generate alerts. You need to minimize query costs while ensuring detection queries run efficiently against 90 days of log data. What should you do?
column3: Use BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate all queries against the log table and create materialized views that pre-compute threat intelligence matches across the full 90-day dataset.
column4: Store threat intelligence indicators as a BigQuery user-defined function (UDF) and call the function in detection queries to avoid JOIN operations against the threat intelligence table.
column5: Configure the sink to route logs to a BigQuery dataset with a 90-day default table expiration and rely on BigQuery automatic optimization for query performance.
column6: Partition the log table by timestamp, create a clustered table on principalEmail and callerIp columns, and use scheduled queries with partition filters that JOIN against the threat intelligence table for detection.
column8: Time-based partitioning limits scanned data to relevant date ranges, clustering on frequently filtered columns improves query performance, and scheduled queries with partition filters ensure cost-effective recurring detections. This configuration optimizes both ad-hoc and automated query patterns. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/clustered-tables

column2: Your organization is planning to deploy VPC Service Controls to protect sensitive BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets. Before enforcing the perimeter, you need to test the configuration to identify potential issues without disrupting production workloads. What should you do?
column3: Configure the service perimeter in dry run mode to log violations without blocking access, then analyze the logged violations before enforcing the perimeter.
column4: Use Cloud IAM Policy Analyzer to simulate perimeter violations before deploying the VPC Service Controls configuration.
column5: Deploy a copy of your production environment and configure an enforced perimeter against the test environment to simulate the expected behavior.
column6: Create the perimeter in enforced mode during off-peak hours and monitor Cloud Audit Logs for access denied errors to identify configuration issues.
column8: Dry run mode logs violations as though the perimeter is enforced but does not prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to identify and resolve potential issues before enabling enforcement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: During an active security incident investigation, your team identifies a compromised service account that has elevated permissions across multiple projects. You need to immediately prevent this service account from performing any actions while your forensic team investigates. You want to implement a solution that cannot be overridden by any allow policies. What should you do?
column3: Create an IAM deny policy at the organization level that denies all permissions to the compromised service account.
column4: Remove all IAM role bindings from the service account across all projects where it has access.
column5: Disable the service account key and delete the service account from the project where it was created.
column6: Apply a VPC Service Controls perimeter around all projects to block API access from the compromised service account.
column8: IAM deny policies override any IAM allow policies and take precedence regardless of what roles are granted to the principal. Attaching the deny policy at the organization level ensures the service account is blocked across all projects. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/deny-overview

column2: Threat hunting"You are building a YARA-L detection rule in Google Security Operations (SecOps) to hunt for threats involving rare or low-prevalence domains accessed by multiple hosts within your environment. You want to optimize the rule for performance and detection accuracy. Which best practice should you follow?
column3: Configure the rule to run only once per day to minimize resource consumption and avoid overwhelming the detection engine.
column4: Omit event type filters to ensure comprehensive coverage across all log sources and maximize threat detection capability.
column5: Place regular expression filters before equality comparisons in the events section to leverage pattern matching optimizations.
column6: Add event type filters at the beginning of the events section to reduce the number of events the rule evaluates and improve performance.
column8: If a YARA-L rule only detects on UDM events of a certain type, adding an event type filter helps optimize the rule by reducing the number of events it needs to evaluate. Google recommends placing these filters at the beginning of the events section for best performance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/yara-l-best-practices

column2: Your organization wants to create a custom Cloud Monitoring dashboard that displays real-time counts of Security Command Center (SCC) findings by severity level. You need to visualize trends in security findings over time, such as the number of critical and high-severity findings detected per hour. What should you do?
column3: Create log-based metrics in Cloud Logging that filter SCC findings by severity, then add metric widgets to a custom Cloud Monitoring dashboard to visualize these metrics over time.
column4: Configure continuous exports from SCC to Pub/Sub, then use BigQuery streaming to directly populate Cloud Monitoring dashboards with severity metrics.
column5: Use the built-in SCC Risk Overview page, which already provides severity-based visualizations, and embed the page directly into Cloud Monitoring.
column6: Enable SCC Premium tier metrics export, which automatically sends finding counts to Cloud Monitoring dashboards without additional configuration.
column8: Log-based metrics allow you to extract numerical data from SCC findings logs, including counts by severity. You can create counter metrics that count entries matching specific criteria such as severity level. These metrics are automatically ingested by Cloud Monitoring and can be visualized in custom dashboards as time-series charts. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics

column2: Your security team is implementing Security Command Center Enterprise and needs to configure automatic case creation for posture findings. The team wants findings to be automatically assigned to the appropriate resource owners. Which sequence correctly describes how the SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector determines resource ownership?
column3: Fallback Owner parameter, then Essential Contacts, then cloud tags if no previous owner is determined.
column4: Cloud tags on the resource, then Essential Contacts inherited from the resource, then the Fallback Owner parameter configured in the connector.
column5: Project owner IAM role assignment, then folder-level Essential Contacts, then organization administrator email address.
column6: Essential Contacts for the project, then IAM policy bindings on the affected resource, then the default service account for the project.
column8: The SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector first analyzes findings for cloud tag values inherited from the finding resource. If no cloud tags exist, it attempts to define the resource owner using Essential Contacts. If neither method identifies an owner, the connector uses the Fallback Owner parameter as a default. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/determine-ownership-posture-findings

column2: Your organization uses Log Analytics in Cloud Logging to analyze security events. You need to create a threat hunting query that identifies any connections to domains on a known malicious domain list maintained in a separate BigQuery table. The domain list is updated daily by your threat intelligence team. What is the most efficient approach to implement this correlation?
column3: Write a Log Analytics SQL query that uses a subquery with the IN operator to check each log entry's domain against a hardcoded list of the malicious domains.
column4: Schedule a Cloud Function to export logs hourly, load them into a separate BigQuery table, and run a scheduled query to join with the threat intelligence table.
column5: Use Log Analytics Query Builder to create filters that match domains from the threat intelligence list by selecting the domain field and specifying match conditions.
column6: Create a linked BigQuery dataset for the log bucket, then write a SQL query that performs an INNER JOIN between the log view and the threat intelligence table on the domain field.
column8: A linked BigQuery dataset enables direct SQL queries that can join log data with other BigQuery tables. The INNER JOIN approach efficiently correlates log entries with the threat intelligence table, returning only matching records. This method leverages BigQuery's optimized join operations for large datasets. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/query-linked-dataset

column2: Observability"You have created a Looker Studio dashboard that displays Security Command Center findings from BigQuery, including critical finding counts, mean time to remediation, and finding severity distribution. Security analysts need to monitor this dashboard continuously on wall-mounted displays in the SOC. You want the dashboard to automatically refresh with the latest data. What should you configure?
column3: Enable auto refresh in the report settings with a refresh interval that matches or exceeds the data source freshness threshold.
column4: Configure a scheduled email delivery of the dashboard to the SOC distribution list every 15 minutes.
column5: Set the data source freshness to 1 minute to ensure the BigQuery connector queries for new data every minute automatically.
column6: Enable embedding mode and configure the embed iframe with JavaScript-based refresh timers.
column8: Auto refresh periodically reloads the report data at the configured interval. To see actual data updates, the auto refresh interval should match or exceed the data source freshness setting, as more frequent refreshes will only return cached data. This configuration supports continuous SOC monitoring use cases. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker-studio/docs/manage-auto-refresh-for-a-report

column2: Your organization has deployed multiple Event Threat Detection custom modules for custom IOC detection. You need to view findings generated by these custom modules separately from the built-in Event Threat Detection findings in Security Command Center. How should you filter the findings?
column3: Query Cloud Audit Logs for custom module creation events and cross-reference with finding timestamps.
column4: Export all findings to BigQuery and write SQL queries to filter by custom module source IDs.
column5: Use the Category filter and search for custom module names since all custom module findings share a common category prefix.
column6: Use the Source display name filter and select 'Event Threat Detection Custom Modules' to display only findings from custom modules.
column8: Security Command Center provides separate source filters for built-in Event Threat Detection detectors and custom modules. You can filter for findings generated by custom modules by selecting 'Event Threat Detection Custom Modules' as the source display name. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-event-threat-detection

column2: Your organization has deployed Google Security Operations (SecOps) and is receiving threat intelligence feeds containing known malicious IP addresses. You need to create a YARA-L detection rule that efficiently checks incoming network traffic against these IP addresses while optimizing rule performance. What should you do?
column3: Use the BigQuery export feature to run SQL queries against ingested logs and compare them with stored IP addresses.
column4: Create a CIDR reference list and use the 'in cidr %reference_list' syntax in your YARA-L rule's events section.
column5: Configure an Applied Threat Intelligence connector to automatically generate detections without creating custom rules.
column6: Write a YARA-L rule with hardcoded IP addresses in multiple OR conditions within the events section.
column8: YARA-L supports CIDR reference lists that allow IP address matching with CIDR notation support. Using '%reference_list' syntax with the 'in cidr' keyword enables efficient IP matching against the threat intelligence feed while optimizing rule performance by reducing events evaluated. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/yara-l/reference-list-syntax

column2: Your security team has detected an active data exfiltration attempt from a compromised service account within a Google Cloud project. The project contains sensitive BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets. You need to immediately contain the incident by preventing data from being copied to unauthorized external locations while maintaining critical business operations. Which containment approach should you implement?
column3: Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter in enforced mode around the affected project with egress rules that only allow data access to explicitly authorized destinations.
column4: Modify the VPC firewall rules to block all outbound traffic from the affected project's network.
column5: Create a VPC Service Controls perimeter in dry-run mode around the affected project to log all potential violations before taking action.
column6: Revoke all IAM permissions for the compromised service account and rely on audit logging to verify containment.
column8: VPC Service Controls perimeters in enforced mode immediately prevent data exfiltration by blocking API requests to restricted services from crossing the perimeter boundary. Egress rules allow you to maintain essential data flows while blocking unauthorized transfers. This provides immediate containment of the exfiltration attempt. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/overview

column2: Your organization has enabled Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) curated detections in Google Security Operations (SecOps). Security analysts report that they are receiving too many alerts for indicators with low confidence. You need to configure ATI to reduce alert noise while maintaining visibility into high-confidence threats. What should you do?
column3: Create custom YARA-L rules that filter ATI IOCs based on GTI Verdict values and disable all curated ATI detections.
column4: Modify the IC-Score threshold in ATI settings to increase the minimum confidence score required for IOC ingestion from 80 to 95.
column5: Enable only the Active Breach Priority and High Priority rule sets from the Curated Prioritization category, and disable the Medium Priority rule sets.
column6: Configure rule exclusions on all ATI curated detections to filter out IOCs that do not have associated threat actor attribution.
column8: Applied Threat Intelligence curated detections include separate rule sets for Active Breach, High, and Medium priority indicators. By enabling only Active Breach and High Priority rule sets, you filter out lower-confidence IOCs while maintaining detection of high-confidence threats from Mandiant threat intelligence. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-curated-detections

column2: You are building a Looker Studio executive dashboard connected to a BigQuery dataset containing Security Command Center findings. The BigQuery export configuration streams new findings in near real-time. However, stakeholders report that the dashboard frequently shows stale data even after new findings are exported to BigQuery. You need to ensure the dashboard displays the most current findings while balancing query costs. What should you configure?
column3: Instruct stakeholders to manually click the refresh button on the dashboard whenever they need updated information.
column4: Adjust the data freshness setting on the BigQuery data source to a shorter interval such as 1 hour to ensure cached data is refreshed more frequently.
column5: Configure the Security Command Center continuous export with a faster export interval to push data to BigQuery more frequently.
column6: Enable BigQuery BI Engine to accelerate dashboard queries and automatically synchronize data with BigQuery.
column8: The data freshness setting determines when Looker Studio considers cached data stale and issues new queries to BigQuery. The default data freshness for BigQuery data sources is 12 hours. Reducing this interval to 1 hour ensures the dashboard displays more current data while still leveraging caching to control query costs. This balances freshness against the cost of frequent queries. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/looker-studio/docs/manage-data-freshness

column2: Your security operations team wants to use Community Security Analytics (CSA) queries to detect privilege escalation attempts in your Google Cloud environment. The queries need to identify when sensitive IAM roles are granted to service accounts by non-approved identities. What should you do first?
column3: Upgrade your centralized log bucket to use Log Analytics and ensure Admin Activity audit logs are being routed to the bucket.
column4: Create a BigQuery sink for audit logs and schedule the CSA queries to run using BigQuery scheduled queries.
column5: Configure Event Threat Detection in Security Command Center to automatically detect IAM anomalies without requiring custom queries.
column6: Enable Data Access audit logs for all services and export them to BigQuery for analysis with CSA queries.
column8: CSA queries require Log Analytics to run SQL against audit logs. Admin Activity audit logs capture IAM policy changes including role grants, and these logs are always written and cannot be disabled. Upgrading the log bucket enables SQL-based analysis of these audit logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/architecture/security-log-analytics

column2: You have deployed a Cloud Function that processes threat intelligence updates from a Pub/Sub topic and initiates automated threat hunting in Google SecOps. The function runs correctly when tested manually but fails when triggered by Eventarc. The logs show 'The request was not authenticated.' You need to resolve this issue. What should you do?
column3: Create a new API key in the Google Cloud project and configure the Eventarc trigger to include the key in request headers.
column4: Modify the Cloud Function to allow unauthenticated invocations by setting the ingress setting to 'Allow all traffic'.
column5: Grant the Cloud Run Invoker role to the service account associated with the Eventarc trigger on the Cloud Function.
column6: Enable the Cloud Functions API and Eventarc API in the project, then recreate the trigger with the default service account.
column8: When an Eventarc trigger invokes an authenticated Cloud Run function (including 2nd gen Cloud Functions), the trigger's service account must have the roles/run.invoker role on the target function. Without this permission, the function rejects the trigger's requests with an authentication error. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/eventarc/docs/roles-permissions

column2: Your security operations team has configured a log-based metric to detect security anomalies and created an alerting policy to monitor it. Analysts report receiving false positive alerts when there are gaps in the log data during off-peak hours. You need to reduce false notifications while maintaining detection effectiveness. What should you do?
column3: Switch from a log-based metric alerting policy to a log-based alerting policy, which does not suffer from data gaps.
column4: Increase the value of the rolling window in the alerting policy to at least 10 minutes and configure how the policy handles missing data in the advanced options.
column5: Create multiple identical alerting policies and require at least two of them to trigger before sending notifications to analysts.
column6: Disable the alerting policy during off-peak hours using a snooze schedule to prevent false positives from occurring.
column8: Log-based metric data can have gaps that result in false notifications. Google Cloud recommends setting the rolling window to at least 10 minutes to ensure multiple log entries are counted, reducing the risk of false positives from data gaps. Additionally, configuring missing data handling in advanced options further mitigates this issue. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics/charts-and-alerts

column2: You have received an urgent threat intelligence alert containing newly discovered IOCs (IP addresses and file hashes) associated with an active threat campaign. You need to immediately determine if any of these IOCs have been observed in your environment's historical data over the past 6 months. Which Google SecOps feature should you use first?
column3: Configure a real-time detection rule with the IOCs and wait for future alerts to indicate ongoing compromise.
column4: Check the IOC Matches page for any previous matches and export the results to a threat intelligence platform for analysis.
column5: Run a retrohunt using a YARA-L rule that matches the IOCs against historical events within the specified time range.
column6: Create a reference list containing the IOCs and configure Applied Threat Intelligence to automatically score matches.
column8: Retrohunt allows you to run a detection rule against historical data stored in Google SecOps, which retains up to 12 months of hot data by default. This enables immediate analysis of whether newly discovered IOCs were present in past events, making it ideal for responding to new threat intelligence about historical compromises. Reference: https://docs.cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your organization has Security Command Center Premium activated at the organization level. You created an Event Threat Detection custom module with a list of suspicious IP addresses at the organization level. A project team wants to add additional IP addresses specific to their project without modifying the organization-level module. What is the correct approach?
column3: Disable the inherited organization-level module at the project level and create a comprehensive project-level module with all IP addresses.
column4: Clone the organization-level custom module to the project and modify it to include both the original and new IP addresses.
column5: Create a new Configurable Bad IP custom module at the project level with the project-specific IP addresses, which will run alongside the inherited organization-level module.
column6: Request the organization security team to update the organization-level module to include the project-specific IP addresses.
column8: Custom modules created at the organization level are inherited by all folders and projects. You can create additional residential custom modules at the project level that run alongside inherited modules. Both modules will scan logs independently, allowing organization-wide and project-specific threat detection. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: Your security team needs to continuously monitor changes to firewall rules and IAM policies across your Google Cloud organization. When a change occurs, you need to trigger automated remediation through a Cloud Function. You want to implement this using Cloud Asset Inventory with minimal operational overhead. What should you do?
column3: Export Cloud Asset Inventory snapshots to BigQuery hourly using scheduled queries, and configure BigQuery to trigger a Cloud Function when new rows are added.
column4: Configure Security Command Center Event Threat Detection to monitor firewall and IAM changes, then use the findings as triggers for Cloud Functions.
column5: Enable Cloud Audit Logs for all IAM and firewall APIs, export logs to Cloud Storage, and create a Cloud Function that periodically scans the storage bucket.
column6: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed that publishes asset change notifications to Pub/Sub, and configure a Cloud Function to subscribe to the Pub/Sub topic.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds provide real-time notifications about resource and policy changes directly to a Pub/Sub topic. You can specify which asset types to monitor, and the messages contain the change details that Cloud Functions can act upon for automated remediation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/monitor-asset-changes

column2: Your security team needs to deploy a new VPC Service Controls perimeter around sensitive BigQuery datasets and Cloud Storage buckets. Before enforcing the perimeter, you want to understand how current application traffic patterns would be affected without disrupting production services. What should you do?
column3: Create the perimeter in dry run mode, analyze the violation logs, and convert to enforced mode after addressing issues.
column4: Create an access level with broad IP ranges, deploy the perimeter in enforced mode, then gradually tighten restrictions.
column5: Create a perimeter bridge between the existing environment and a test project to evaluate traffic flow patterns.
column6: Create the perimeter in enforced mode with all access levels configured and monitor Cloud Audit Logs for errors.
column8: Dry run mode logs violations as though the perimeter is enforced but does not prevent access to restricted services. This allows you to understand the impact of the perimeter configuration, identify required exceptions, and validate that application traffic patterns will work correctly before enforcement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc-service-controls/docs/dry-run-mode

column2: Incident response"During an active incident investigation in Google Security Operations (SecOps), you discover a new malicious file hash from forensic analysis that was not previously in your threat intelligence feeds. You need to determine if this hash appeared in your environment in the past 90 days. What is the most effective approach to search for this IOC across historical log data?
column3: Submit the hash to Google Threat Intelligence for analysis and configure an alert to notify when matches are found.
column4: Add the hash to a custom reference list and wait for the live detection rules to identify any new matches in incoming data.
column5: Export 90 days of raw logs from Google SecOps to Cloud Storage and use grep to search for the hash pattern.
column6: Create a YARA-L detection rule that matches on the file hash and run a retrohunt against the past 90 days of ingested data.
column8: A retrohunt allows you to use a YARA-L rule to search for detections throughout existing historical data in Google SecOps. This is the most effective method to identify past occurrences of a newly discovered IOC across your environment logs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/run-rule-historical-data

column2: Your security team has deployed Container Threat Detection across all GKE clusters. After enabling it, analysts report that they are not receiving findings for suspicious file access to /etc/shadow on container hosts. You have verified that the GKE version supports Container Threat Detection. What is the most likely cause of this issue?
column3: The Container Threat Detection service account is missing the required containerthreatdetection.serviceAgent role.
column4: The Container Threat Detection DaemonSet has not been deployed to the nodes where the suspicious activity occurred.
column5: The GKE clusters are using GKE Sandbox, which is incompatible with Container Threat Detection.
column6: The file monitoring detectors are disabled by default and must be manually enabled in the Container Threat Detection module settings.
column8: Container Threat Detection includes file monitoring detectors that monitor file operations looking for access or modification to critical system files. However, these detectors are disabled by default because workloads with significant file I/O could potentially suffer performance degradation when enabled. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-container-threat-detection-overview

column2: Your security team is configuring Event Threat Detection custom modules to detect connections to known command-and-control (C2) server IP addresses. They want findings from these detections to be prioritized for immediate response. How should they configure the severity level in the custom module JSON template?
column3: Create a separate SCC notification configuration to route all custom module findings to a high-priority Pub/Sub topic regardless of severity.
column4: Use security marks to tag all custom module findings as high-priority after they are generated.
column5: Configure the detectionPriority field in the sourceProperties to HIGH for all C2-related findings.
column6: Set the severity parameter to CRITICAL in the metadata section of the custom module JSON template.
column8: Custom module templates allow you to define severity levels (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, or CRITICAL) in the metadata section. Setting severity to CRITICAL ensures findings from C2 server connections are prioritized appropriately for immediate incident response. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/use-custom-modules-etd

column2: You need to configure Google SecOps SOAR to ingest findings from Security Command Center (SCC) and automatically trigger investigation playbooks. After installing the Google Security Command Center integration from the Content Hub, what additional configuration steps are required?
column3: Configure the SCC Findings connector with appropriate parameters and create playbook triggers that match the SCC product name.
column4: Configure service account credentials in the integration settings and the integration will automatically create the required connector.
column5: Enable the SCC API in Google Cloud Console and configure a Cloud Function to push findings to SOAR.
column6: Create a webhook endpoint in SOAR and configure SCC to send findings notifications to the webhook URL.
column8: After installing an integration, connectors must be separately configured to ingest alerts. The connector translates SCC findings into normalized SOAR data. Playbook triggers using Product Name ensure playbooks attach to alerts originating from the SCC connector. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-configure-secops-soar

column2: Your organization has VPC Flow Logs enabled across multiple subnets in a production environment. You need to configure the logs optimally for security threat hunting while managing storage costs. The security team requires sufficient granularity to detect lateral movement patterns that may occur within short time windows. Which VPC Flow Logs configuration best balances detection capability with cost efficiency?
column3: Set the aggregation interval to 5 seconds with a sampling rate of 50% and include all metadata annotations for enriched context during analysis.
column4: Set the aggregation interval to 15 minutes with a sampling rate of 100% and exclude all metadata to minimize log volume and storage costs.
column5: Set the aggregation interval to 1 minute with a sampling rate of 5% and include custom metadata limited to source and destination IP only.
column6: Set the aggregation interval to 30 seconds with a sampling rate of 100% and configure log filtering to capture only denied traffic for security analysis.
column8: A 5-second aggregation interval provides the granularity needed to detect rapid lateral movement patterns such as port scanning, which can occur in short bursts. A 50% sampling rate balances cost with visibility, and including metadata annotations provides essential context like VM names and project information for threat investigation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/using-flow-logs

column2: Threat hunting"Your organization has Security Command Center Enterprise tier activated. Security analysts have noticed that Event Threat Detection generates many findings, but they struggle to determine which findings represent the highest-risk threats requiring immediate investigation. You want to correlate SCC threat findings with additional context from Cloud Audit Logs and threat intelligence for better prioritization. What should you do?
column3: Use SCC's Risk Engine to generate attack exposure scores for all threat findings and prioritize based on toxic combination detection.
column4: Configure continuous exports from SCC to Pub/Sub and create Cloud Functions to enrich findings with VirusTotal data before storing in BigQuery.
column5: Enable all Event Threat Detection custom modules and configure alert severity thresholds to filter only critical and high findings.
column6: Ingest SCC findings into Chronicle and enable the CDIR SCC Enhanced rule sets, which correlate SCC threat findings with Cloud Audit Logs and threat intelligence data.
column8: The CDIR SCC Enhanced rule sets contain context-aware rules that correlate Security Command Center findings with other log sources. For example, CDIR SCC Enhanced Malware correlates SCC Malware findings with IP addresses, domains, and prevalence scores from threat intelligence, along with Cloud DNS logs. This provides the contextual correlation needed for better prioritization. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/cloud-threats-category

column2: Your security team has deployed a threat hunting automation system using Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub. The function processes newly published IOCs and queries Google SecOps SIEM for matches in historical data. During testing, you observe that the function occasionally receives duplicate IOC messages, causing redundant API calls and increased costs. What is the recommended approach to handle this scenario?
column3: Set the acknowledgment deadline to the maximum value of 600 seconds to ensure the function completes processing before any redelivery occurs.
column4: Design the Cloud Function to be idempotent by checking if the IOC has already been processed using a unique message identifier before initiating the threat hunt.
column5: Enable exactly-once delivery on the Pub/Sub subscription to guarantee each IOC message is delivered and processed only once.
column6: Configure message ordering on the Pub/Sub subscription using ordering keys to prevent duplicate delivery of IOC messages.
column8: Pub/Sub provides at-least-once delivery, meaning duplicate messages can occur. The recommended best practice is to design idempotent handlers that can safely process the same message multiple times without adverse effects. Using unique identifiers from the message or its attributes allows deduplication. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/exactly-once-delivery

column2: Your organization has set a list constraint at the organization level that denies a specific Cloud Storage location. A project owner needs to add additional denied locations at the project level while maintaining the restrictions from the organization. You need to configure the project-level organization policy to achieve this. What should you do?
column3: Reset the project-level policy to Google-managed default behavior and modify the organization-level policy to include all required denied values.
column4: Set the project-level organization policy with only the additional denied values and select the Replace option to override parent's policy.
column5: Create a custom constraint at the project level with the additional denied values and let the organization policy remain unchanged.
column6: Set the project-level organization policy with the additional denied values and set inheritFromParent to true.
column8: Setting inheritFromParent to true for list constraints causes the effective policy of the parent resource to be inherited, merged, and reconciled with the child resource's policy. This allows the project to add additional denied values while maintaining the organization-level restrictions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/understanding-hierarchy

column2: You need to create an alerting policy that monitors for complex security patterns across aggregated log data, such as detecting when more than 100 failed authentication attempts occur from the same source IP address within a 30-minute window. The log bucket has been upgraded to use Log Analytics. What additional requirement must be met before you can create this alerting policy?
column3: Create a linked BigQuery dataset for the log bucket because SQL-based alerting policies require data to be accessible through a linked dataset.
column4: Create a log-based metric to pre-aggregate the authentication failures before configuring the SQL-based alerting policy.
column5: Configure custom labels on the log entries to enable aggregation by source IP address.
column6: Enable the Cloud Monitoring API because SQL-based alerting policies are managed through Cloud Monitoring.
column8: SQL-based alerting policies run on the BigQuery engine, which requires the data being queried to be accessible through a linked BigQuery dataset. The log bucket must be upgraded to Log Analytics and then a linked dataset must be created before SQL-based alerting policies can be configured. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/sql-in-alerting

column2: Your security team uses Security Command Center Enterprise and has identified several Security Health Analytics findings that are expected behavior for your development environment. The team wants to prevent these findings from creating cases and complicating analyst workflows. You need to implement a solution that also allows viewing these findings for audit purposes. What should you do?
column3: Create dynamic mute rules for the findings matching the expected behavior criteria, which will prevent them from appearing in cases while maintaining audit logs.
column4: Configure the SCC Enterprise - Urgent Posture Findings Connector to exclude findings from the development environment based on project ID filters.
column5: Mark the findings as resolved in the case management system and configure playbooks to auto-close cases containing only development environment findings.
column6: Disable the specific Security Health Analytics detectors that generate the findings for the development environment projects.
column8: Muting findings prevents them from appearing in cases in Security Command Center Enterprise. Dynamic mute rules are recommended because they offer more flexibility, and muted findings continue to be logged for audit and compliance purposes. If all findings in a case are muted, the case automatically closes. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/mute-findings-in-cases

column2: You are designing a forensic investigation playbook in Google SecOps SOAR that automatically collects disk snapshots and memory dumps when malware is detected on a Compute Engine VM. The evidence must be stored in a way that prevents modification or deletion for at least 90 days to meet legal hold requirements. Which Cloud Storage configuration should you implement?
column3: Create a dedicated forensic bucket with Object Versioning enabled and configure lifecycle rules to retain all object versions for 90 days.
column4: Create a dedicated forensic bucket and apply a temporary hold on each evidence object uploaded by the playbook.
column5: Create a dedicated forensic bucket with a 90-day retention policy, then lock the retention policy to prevent any modifications or early deletion of evidence.
column6: Create a dedicated forensic bucket with IAM Deny policies that prevent deletion permissions for all users except the forensic team.
column8: Bucket Lock with a locked retention policy ensures that objects cannot be deleted or modified until they reach the specified retention period. Once locked, the retention policy cannot be reduced or removed, providing the immutability guarantees required for legal hold scenarios. This meets regulatory and compliance requirements for forensic evidence preservation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: You are investigating a potential data exfiltration incident using Google Security Operations (SecOps). You have identified a suspicious domain that was not previously in any threat intelligence feeds. You want to search across your historical network events to identify all assets that communicated with this domain and understand the timeline of connections. What is the most efficient approach?
column3: Use the Domain view in Google SecOps to search for the suspicious domain and review the asset timeline showing all historical connections.
column4: Create a YARA-L rule matching the domain, enable it as a live rule, and wait for future detections to appear.
column5: Submit the domain to Google Threat Intelligence and wait for it to be added to the Applied Threat Intelligence feed.
column6: Export your network logs to BigQuery and use SQL queries to search for the domain across the exported dataset.
column8: The Domain view in Google SecOps allows you to investigate specific domains and see what impact they have on your assets. It provides a timeline view of all assets that communicated with the domain, making it ideal for investigating unknown suspicious domains not yet in threat feeds. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/overview

column2: Your organization has an Organization Policy constraint set at the organization level that restricts the creation of external IP addresses on Compute Engine instances (constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess). A development folder requires an exception to allow external IP addresses for specific testing purposes. The folder's policy should also retain some restrictions from the parent organization policy while adding new allowed values. What should you configure at the folder level to achieve this?
column3: Select 'Override parent's policy' and set 'Replace' under Policy enforcement, then add all required values including parent values.
column4: Select 'Google-managed default' and configure a separate custom constraint for the folder.
column5: Select 'Inherit parent's policy' and add conditional rules with tags for the testing environment.
column6: Select 'Override parent's policy' and set 'Merge with parent' under Policy enforcement, then add the required allowed values.
column8: When you select 'Override parent's policy' and choose 'Merge with parent,' the effective policy on the folder will merge with the parent organization's policy. This allows you to add additional allowed values at the folder level while retaining inherited restrictions from the parent policy. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/understanding-hierarchy

column2: Your organization wants to test Container Threat Detection to validate that it is properly configured before relying on it for production workload security. You need to trigger a detection and verify that findings appear in Security Command Center. What is the recommended approach to test Container Threat Detection?
column3: Submit a test request through the Security Command Center API to generate synthetic Container Threat Detection findings for validation.
column4: Deploy a test container with a name prefixed with 'ktd-test' and execute a known suspicious behavior such as running a reverse shell or accessing sensitive host files.
column5: Disable the Container Threat Detection noise reduction filter globally and deploy any container with standard behaviors to verify telemetry collection.
column6: Enable verbose logging mode for Container Threat Detection and analyze the raw telemetry output for expected detection events.
column8: Google recommends prefixing the container or pod name with 'ktd-test' when testing Container Threat Detection. This bypasses noise reduction filters that temporarily filter certain findings for new containers. You can then execute known malicious behaviors like running reverse shells or reading /etc/shadow to trigger detections. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-test-container-threat-detection

column2: You need to detect when critical security log sources stop sending data to Cloud Logging, which could indicate a compromised or misconfigured system. You want to create an alerting mechanism that notifies your security team when a specific log source has not written any data for 30 minutes after having previously sent data. What should you configure?
column3: Create a metric-absence alerting policy that monitors the log-based metric for the specific log source with a 30-minute trigger absence time.
column4: Create a SQL-based alerting policy that queries for zero log entries from the source within a 30-minute sliding window.
column5: Create a log-based alerting policy that searches for the absence of specific log entry patterns within 30 minutes.
column6: Create a counter metric and configure an alerting policy with a threshold condition of less than one over 30 minutes.
column8: Metric-absence conditions notify you when a monitored time series has no data for a specific period. The trigger absence time specifies how long the metric must be absent before alerting. This requires at least one successful measurement before the absence detection activates. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/monitoring/alerts/metric-absence

column2: Your security team needs to centralize audit logs from all 50 projects within your Google Cloud organization into a single BigQuery dataset for security analysis. The logs must include Admin Activity and Data Access audit logs from all projects, and the team wants to prevent child projects from storing duplicate copies locally. Which configuration should you implement?
column3: Create individual project-level sinks in all 50 projects with identical filters and configure each to export to the same BigQuery dataset with partitioned tables.
column4: Create an intercepting aggregated sink at the organization level with a filter for audit logs and configure the destination as a BigQuery dataset with partitioned tables.
column5: Create a non-intercepting aggregated sink at the folder level for each business unit and configure each to export to separate BigQuery datasets with date-sharded tables.
column6: Create a non-intercepting aggregated sink at the organization level with a filter for audit logs and configure the destination as a BigQuery dataset with date-sharded tables.
column8: An intercepting aggregated sink routes log entries from all child resources (projects and folders) within the organization while preventing those logs from being routed to sinks in child resources, except for _Required sinks. This prevents duplicate storage. Partitioned tables are recommended for better query performance. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/aggregated_sinks

column2: Your security team has identified that some developers in your organization need to deploy Compute Engine instances that run with a dedicated service account. The developers should not be able to impersonate the service account using the gcloud CLI or create short-lived credentials directly. You need to configure the minimum required permissions following the principle of least privilege. Which IAM role should you grant to the developers on the service account?
column3: Service Account Token Creator (roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator)
column4: Service Account Admin (roles/iam.serviceAccountAdmin)
column5: Project Editor (roles/editor)
column6: Service Account User (roles/iam.serviceAccountUser)
column8: The Service Account User role lets a principal attach a service account to a resource, such as a Compute Engine instance. When code running on that resource needs to authenticate, it can get credentials for the attached service account. This role does not allow principals to create short-lived credentials for service accounts or to use the --impersonate-service-account flag for the gcloud CLI. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/service-account-permissions

column2: Your forensic investigation playbook requires uploading disk images from compromised VMs to Cloud Storage for offline analysis. The disk images may contain sensitive data and must be protected during upload and storage. You need to ensure the evidence maintains chain of custody requirements and cannot be accessed by unauthorized parties. What should you configure for the forensic evidence bucket?
column3: Configure Google-managed encryption, enable Object Versioning, and restrict bucket access using IAM deny policies.
column4: Enable customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) for the bucket, configure Object Retention Lock in Locked mode, and enable Data Access audit logs.
column5: Enable uniform bucket-level access, configure signed URLs for uploads, and set the bucket to private with no public access.
column6: Enable customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEK) for all uploads, configure Bucket Lock with a 365-day retention period, and use VPC Service Controls.
column8: CMEK provides control over encryption key management and can support key rotation or revocation if needed. Object Retention Lock in Locked mode ensures evidence cannot be deleted or modified, supporting chain of custody requirements. Data Access audit logs create a record of all access attempts to the evidence, supporting forensic integrity. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/object-lock

column2: Your security team needs to create custom dashboards in Cloud Monitoring to visualize Security Command Center (SCC) findings over time. The dashboard should display trends for high-severity findings detected by Event Threat Detection and Container Threat Detection. Which approach should you use to enable this visualization?
column3: Configure SCC Premium to automatically push metrics to Cloud Monitoring dashboards through the built-in SCC-Monitoring integration feature.
column4: Stream SCC findings directly to Cloud Monitoring using the Security Command Center metrics API and create charts from the securitycenter.googleapis.com/findings metric type.
column5: Configure continuous exports for SCC findings to Cloud Logging, create log-based metrics from the exported findings, and add charts using those metrics to a custom Cloud Monitoring dashboard.
column6: Use the Cloud Monitoring API to directly query the SCC findings database and configure custom metric descriptors that pull finding counts in real time.
column8: SCC findings from Event Threat Detection and Container Threat Detection can be exported to Cloud Logging using continuous exports, which then allows you to create log-based metrics that track finding occurrences. These log-based metrics can be displayed in Cloud Monitoring charts and dashboards, enabling trend visualization over time. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/export-cloud-logging

column2: Your incident response team is investigating a Cloud SQL data exfiltration alert from Security Command Center. The finding indicates that database data was exported to a Cloud Storage bucket outside your organization. You need to collect evidence about who performed the export and when. Which Cloud Logging query approach should you use?
column3: Query Cloud Monitoring metrics for Cloud SQL export operations and correlate with IAM authentication events.
column4: Create a custom log sink to export all Cloud SQL audit logs to BigQuery and run SQL queries to search for export operations in the last 30 days.
column5: Enable Data Access audit logs for Cloud SQL and wait for new export events to be captured for correlation analysis.
column6: Navigate to Logs Explorer using the Cloud Logging URI from the Security Command Center finding to view pre-filtered logs related to the Cloud SQL export operation.
column8: Security Command Center exfiltration findings include a Cloud Logging URI that links directly to pre-filtered log entries related to the incident. This provides the fastest path to relevant evidence including the principal email, timestamp, and export scope details. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/findings/threats/cloudsql-exfil-export

column2: Your security team suspects lateral movement within your Google Cloud environment after a VM compromise was detected. You need to identify all VMs that the compromised VM (10.10.0.5) communicated with over the last 24 hours using VPC Flow Logs exported to BigQuery. Which BigQuery query approach should you use?
column3: Query the VPC Flow Logs table filtering on protocol=6 only to capture SSH sessions between the compromised VM and other hosts.
column4: Query the Cloud Audit Logs table for the VM's network interface and filter by methodName to identify all outbound API calls made by the instance.
column5: Query the VPC Flow Logs table filtering on the src_ip field for 10.10.0.5 and aggregate by dest_ip to identify unique destination hosts across internal IP ranges.
column6: Use the bytes_sent field in VPC Flow Logs to calculate total data transfer and identify the VM with highest inbound traffic from the compromised host.
column8: VPC Flow Logs contain the 5-tuple information (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol) that allows you to filter by the compromised VM's source IP address and identify all unique destination IPs it communicated with. Aggregating by dest_ip reveals the scope of potential lateral movement. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/vpc/docs/about-flow-logs-records

column2: Your organization is deploying applications on GKE and wants to ensure each microservice can only access the specific Google Cloud resources it requires. You need to configure workload-level identity management following least privilege principles. Which configuration approach should you implement?
column3: Enable Workload Identity Federation for GKE, create unique Kubernetes ServiceAccounts for each microservice, and grant IAM roles on specific resources to each ServiceAccount's principal identifier.
column4: Use the Compute Engine default service account for all node pools and grant it all necessary roles at the project level.
column5: Create one IAM service account per namespace with all required permissions, and configure all pods in the namespace to use that service account through annotation.
column6: Generate service account keys for each microservice and mount them as Kubernetes secrets in the respective pods.
column8: Workload Identity Federation for GKE lets you assign distinct, fine-grained identities to each application by using IAM policies with Kubernetes ServiceAccount principal identifiers. Granting IAM roles at the resource level ensures each microservice only accesses the specific resources it needs. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/workload-identity

column2: Your organization wants to monitor for potential brute-force login attempts across your Google Cloud environment. You need to be alerted when there are more than 50 failed authentication attempts from a single IP address within a 15-minute window. The solution must aggregate data across multiple log entries before triggering an alert. What should you do?
column3: Configure a log sink to export authentication logs to Pub/Sub and write a Cloud Function to count failures and send alerts via email when thresholds are exceeded.
column4: Create a counter-type log-based metric that counts authentication failures, then configure an alerting policy with a threshold condition of 50 events.
column5: Create a log-based alerting policy in the Logs Explorer that filters for authentication failure messages and configures the time between notifications to 15 minutes.
column6: Upgrade the log bucket to use Log Analytics with a linked BigQuery dataset, then create a SQL-based alerting policy that queries authentication failures grouped by IP address.
column8: SQL-based alerting policies can monitor aggregate analysis of log entry data by running SQL queries against log views. This approach supports complex patterns like counting and grouping failed authentication attempts from specific IP addresses within defined time windows. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/analyze/sql-in-alerting

column2: Your security team needs to receive real-time notifications whenever IAM policies are modified on production projects in your Google Cloud organization. You want to automate remediation actions when unauthorized changes occur. What should you configure?
column3: Enable Security Command Center asset discovery and configure continuous export to stream all IAM policy changes to a Cloud Storage bucket for processing.
column4: Create a Cloud Asset Inventory feed with the IAM_POLICY content type and configure it to publish notifications to a Pub/Sub topic, then trigger a Cloud Function to perform remediation.
column5: Use Security Command Center Event Threat Detection to monitor for IAM policy anomalies and configure automatic notification workflows.
column6: Configure Cloud Audit Logs to capture SetIamPolicy events and export them to a Pub/Sub topic using a log sink.
column8: Cloud Asset Inventory feeds provide real-time notifications for asset changes. By specifying the IAM_POLICY content type, you receive notifications whenever IAM policy bindings change. Publishing to Pub/Sub allows you to trigger automated remediation through Cloud Functions. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/asset-inventory/docs/monitor-asset-changes

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center (SCC) Enterprise tier and wants to enhance threat detection by correlating SCC Event Threat Detection findings with Cloud Audit Logs and other data sources in Google SecOps. You need to implement detection rules that identify complex attack patterns combining SCC findings with additional context. What should you do?
column3: Enable CDIR SCC Enhanced rule sets in Google SecOps curated detections to correlate SCC findings with Cloud Audit Logs and other Google Cloud data sources.
column4: Use the SCC API to pull findings and manually create correlation rules in a custom SIEM solution outside of Google SecOps.
column5: Configure SCC to export findings directly to BigQuery and create scheduled queries to correlate findings with Cloud Audit Logs.
column6: Create custom Event Threat Detection modules in SCC that directly query Cloud Audit Logs for correlation during threat detection.
column8: CDIR (Cloud Detection, Investigation, and Response) SCC Enhanced rule sets contain context-aware rules that correlate Security Command Center findings with data from other sources including Cloud Audit Logs. These rules are specifically designed to enhance threat detection by combining SCC findings with additional context from multiple log sources. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/cloud-threats-category

column2: Your organization's security operations team has detected a compromised VM in a production VPC network. You need to immediately isolate the VM to prevent lateral movement while preserving evidence for forensic investigation. The VM must remain powered on for live memory acquisition. What should you do?
column3: Disable the network interface of the compromised VM using the Compute Engine API to immediately sever network connectivity.
column4: Use VPC Service Controls to add the project containing the compromised VM to a new service perimeter with restricted API access.
column5: Delete the external IP address from the VM and move the VM to a quarantine subnet with no routes to other networks.
column6: Apply a network tag to the compromised VM and create a high-priority VPC firewall rule with deny action for all ingress and egress traffic targeting that tag.
column8: Applying a network tag and creating high-priority deny firewall rules allows immediate isolation at the network level while keeping the VM running. VPC firewall rules are enforced at the instance level regardless of OS configuration, preventing the compromised VM from bypassing isolation. This approach preserves volatile evidence for live forensics. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/firewall/docs/firewalls

column2: Your security operations team needs to monitor Cloud Logging for anomalies and wants to understand the differences between system-defined and user-defined log-based metrics for security monitoring. Which statement accurately describes the behavior of these metric types?
column3: User-defined log-based metrics can be created at the organization level, while system-defined metrics apply only to individual projects.
column4: System-defined log-based metrics provide real-time alerting on individual log entries, while user-defined metrics require aggregation over time windows.
column5: System-defined log-based metrics automatically populate historical data, while user-defined metrics only count log entries received after creation.
column6: User-defined log-based metrics are calculated from both included and excluded logs, while system-defined metrics are calculated only from included logs stored in log buckets.
column8: User-defined log-based metrics are calculated from all log entries received by the Logging API, regardless of inclusion or exclusion filters that may apply. System-defined log-based metrics are calculated only from log entries that have been stored in log buckets, so explicitly excluded logs are not included in system metrics. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/logs-based-metrics

column2: Your organization needs to enforce that all new Cloud Storage buckets across all projects require uniform bucket-level access. You want to verify the current effective policy on a specific project that may have inherited or overridden policies from parent resources. Which gcloud command should you use?
column3: gcloud org-policies describe constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess --effective --project=PROJECT_ID
column4: gcloud org-policies describe constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess --project=PROJECT_ID
column5: gcloud resource-manager org-policies describe constraints/storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess --project=PROJECT_ID
column6: gcloud org-policies list --project=PROJECT_ID --filter='constraint:storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess'
column8: The --effective flag returns the organization policy as it is evaluated at that specific point in the resource hierarchy with all inheritance included. This shows the actual policy that will be enforced on the project, whether it was set directly, inherited, or merged from parent resources. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/using-constraints

column2: Your organization's SOC team received an alert from Google Security Operations (SecOps) SIEM indicating a potential malware infection. The Applied Threat Intelligence (ATI) feature identified an IOC match with a High priority based on Mandiant threat intelligence. You need to investigate this incident to understand the scope and impact. What should you do first?
column3: Use BigQuery to export all logs from the past 30 days and perform offline analysis to identify all assets communicating with the malicious indicator.
column4: Navigate to the IOC matches page and review the Events tab to view event prioritization, UDM fields, and event details related to the IOC match.
column5: Create a new YARA-L rule to detect the IOC and enable it as a live rule to capture future instances of this threat pattern.
column6: Immediately mute the IOC to prevent alert fatigue while the investigation is pending to reduce noise for other analysts.
column8: When Applied Threat Intelligence is enabled and an IOC match occurs, the IOC matches page displays all relevant details. The Events tab shows how events are prioritized, provides the rationale for the priority, and displays the UDM fields and event details needed to understand the incident scope. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/detection/ati-view-ioc-page

column2: Your security team has identified that several incident response playbooks share identical enrichment and notification logic. You want to centralize this common workflow to reduce maintenance overhead and ensure consistency across all playbooks. What should you do?
column3: Create a playbook block containing the shared enrichment and notification actions, then incorporate this block into the parent playbooks where this logic is needed.
column4: Export the enrichment playbook as a JSON file and import it as a nested playbook reference in each parent playbook that requires the shared logic.
column5: Create a master playbook that all alerts trigger first, which then calls the appropriate response playbook based on alert type.
column6: Use environment variables to store the enrichment logic, and reference these variables in each playbook to maintain consistency.
column8: Playbook blocks are reusable mini-playbooks designed specifically for this use case. Any edit to a block automatically affects all playbooks that incorporate it, reducing maintenance overhead and ensuring consistency. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/chronicle/docs/soar/respond/working-with-playbooks/working-with-playbook-blocks

column2: Your legal team has requested that you preserve all Cloud Audit Logs related to an ongoing investigation in Cloud Storage for a minimum of 7 years. The logs must not be deletable or modifiable by anyone, including administrators, until the retention period expires. Which Cloud Storage feature configuration should you implement?
column3: Configure a retention policy on the bucket and lock the retention policy to make it permanent and immutable.
column4: Enable Object Versioning on the bucket and configure lifecycle rules to prevent deletion of versions.
column5: Configure IAM policies to deny the storage.objects.delete permission for all users including administrators.
column6: Set a temporary hold on all objects uploaded to the bucket using a Cloud Function triggered by object creation.
column8: Locking a bucket's retention policy permanently prevents the policy from being removed or the retention period from being reduced. Once locked, objects cannot be deleted until they meet the retention period, providing the immutable storage required for legal evidence preservation. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/bucket-lock

column2: You are updating the SCC Enterprise – Cloud Orchestration and Remediation use case in Security Command Center Enterprise to support the latest toxic combination functionality. The update process requires modifying the existing connector configuration. What is the correct sequence of steps to update the SCC Enterprise – Urgent Posture Findings Connector without losing pending findings?
column3: Install the new use case version first, which will automatically update the connector and all associated playbooks without requiring any manual intervention.
column4: Delete and recreate the connector with the new configuration settings, then manually reimport all findings from the last 24 hours using the SCC API.
column5: Create a backup of the existing connector configuration, delete the connector, install the new use case, and restore the connector from the backup configuration.
column6: Disable the connector, delete the existing default playbooks, install the latest use case version, update the connector parameters, and re-enable the connector.
column8: Security Command Center ingests findings collected while the connector is disabled when you update and enable the connector. You must disable the connector before deleting playbooks to avoid having alerts with no playbooks attached. Deleting playbooks before upgrading prevents duplication and has no impact on case management. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/enterprise-security-operations-software-update

column2: Your security operations center uses an external threat intelligence platform that provides daily updates of malicious IP addresses. You want to configure Event Threat Detection to detect connections to these IP addresses. However, you discover that the Configurable Bad IP custom module is generating findings based on VPC network traffic. What is the most likely reason if the module fails to detect connections to the threat intelligence IPs?
column3: VPC Flow Logs are not enabled for the VPCs containing the monitored resources, preventing the custom module from detecting the network connections.
column4: The Security Command Center Standard tier does not support custom modules, requiring an upgrade to the Premium tier.
column5: Event Threat Detection custom modules cannot use external threat intelligence sources and only support Google-provided threat indicators.
column6: The threat intelligence IP addresses exceed the 6 MB custom module size limit causing the module to fail silently.
column8: The Configurable Bad IP custom module requires VPC Flow Logs (or alternatively Cloud NAT logging or Firewall Rules Logging) to detect connections to suspicious IP addresses. If VPC Flow Logs are not enabled, the custom module cannot evaluate network traffic to generate findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/concepts-event-threat-detection-overview

column2: You are investigating a potential privilege escalation incident and need to analyze Cloud Audit Logs to understand the full sequence of events. You want to identify both the API calls that modified IAM policies and the subsequent data access patterns. Which combination of audit log types must you analyze?
column3: Data Access audit logs for IAM policy reads, and Policy Denied audit logs for unauthorized access attempts.
column4: Admin Activity audit logs only, since they record all administrative operations including data access by administrators.
column5: System Event audit logs for all automated actions and Policy Denied audit logs for access violations.
column6: Admin Activity audit logs for IAM policy changes, and Data Access audit logs for subsequent resource access patterns.
column8: Admin Activity audit logs capture API calls that modify configuration including SetIamPolicy operations, while Data Access audit logs record API calls that read or access user data. Analyzing both provides the complete attack chain from privilege escalation to data exfiltration. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/logging/docs/audit

column2: A security analyst notices that after disabling a Security Health Analytics detector, the existing active findings for that detector type remain visible in Security Command Center. The analyst expects the findings to be removed immediately. What explains this behavior?
column3: Security Health Analytics operates using batch scans, so the change takes effect only after all ongoing batch scans complete.
column4: The default Findings page filter shows both active and inactive findings, so the findings appear unchanged.
column5: Findings are only removed after a manual purge is triggered through the Security Command Center Settings page.
column6: When a detector is disabled, existing findings are automatically marked as inactive, not deleted, and remain visible in Security Command Center.
column8: Disabling Security Health Analytics detectors changes the state of existing findings to INACTIVE rather than deleting them. Findings in Security Command Center are retained according to the data retention policy and can be viewed by adjusting query filters to show inactive findings. Reference: https://cloud.google.com/security-command-center/docs/how-to-use-security-health-analytics

column2: Your organization uses Security Command Center Premium and wants to prioritize vulnerability remediation based on real-world exploitability data. You notice that some vulnerability findings have CVE information with exploitability ratings. What is the source of these exploitability ratings and how do they affect vulnerability prioritization?
column3: The exploitability ratings are calculated by the Risk Engine during attack path simulations and are only available for toxic combination findings.
column4: The exploitability ratings are provided by Mandiant Threat Intelligence analysts and are incorporated into attack exposure score calculations to provide more accurate prioritization.
column5: The exploitability ratings are sourced from the National Vulnerability Database (NVD) CVSS scores and are displayed as informational metadata only.
column6: The exploitability ratings are generated by Security Health Analytics based on network exposure and are used to filter findings on the Vulnerabilities page.
column8: Security Command Center includes CVE exploitability ratings provided by Mandiant Threat Intelligence analysts in vulnerability finding details.
